paragraphs.text: Lesson 44, common slang.
Slang is not usually taught in textbooks, and you won't hear it in academic or professional
situations.
But in movies, TV shows, and informal conversations, these words are used frequently.
In today's lesson, you're going to learn 15 common slang words used in American English.
Number one, awesome means great, wonderful, or impressive.
You can use the word awesome as an adjective to describe almost anything, like an object,
an experience, an accomplishment, or an action.
Listen to these examples.
Did you see his new motorcycle?
It's awesome.
I just got back from an awesome trip to Europe.
Congratulations on your promotion.
That's awesome.
That organization is doing some awesome work in the poor neighborhoods of the city.
Number two, big deal.
Big deal can mean an important event, or not an important event.
This expression changes meaning depending on how you say it.
Compare these two dialogues.
I'm going to be interviewed on local TV.
Congratulations.
That's a big deal.
I'm going to be interviewed on local TV.
Big deal.
I'm going to be interviewed on national TV.
In the first case, big deal describes an important event or accomplishment.
And in the second case, big deal is used sarcastically to mean the opposite thing, to say that something
is not important or impressive.
Number three, bombed means failed.
But the bomb means great.
If you say that movie bombed, it means the movie was a failure.
It was not popular or successful.
But if you say that movie was the bomb, it means the movie was fantastic.
Number four, bogus means fake, not valid.
Sometimes teenagers try to buy alcohol using a bogus ID, a fake document that shows that
they are over 21 years old, although they're not.
Number five, buddies, pals, and the crew all mean friends.
You can say, I went surfing with a bunch of my buddies, or Bob and I became pals after
we did some volunteer work together.
The crew is often used to refer to friends that are part of a specific group.
For example, if you are part of a basketball team, you can say, I went out with the basketball
crew.
Some people also use the crew to refer to their general group of friends who spend time together
frequently.
Number six, bummer means something unfortunate.
Bummer is used to say, that's too bad, or that's unlucky or unfortunate.
For example,
I won't be able to meet you guys at the bar.
My boss has asked me to work until eight.
Bummer.
Other variations of the phrase are, that's a real bummer, or that's such a bummer.
We usually use this for small or common things, not major tragedies.
If someone tells you, I was just diagnosed with cancer, don't say bummer, because it sounds
insensitive.
Instead, you can say one of the condolence phrases, like, I'm so sorry to hear that.
Number seven, dude means man.
Dude is a generic word for man.
It can't be used for a woman.
Often when we don't know who the person is, or when talking about men in general.
For example, some dude at the party drank too much and got taken to the hospital.
I use dude here because I don't know the man.
My sister always dates athletic dudes.
Athletic dudes means athletic men in general.
Number eight, busted means discovered doing something wrong or illegal.
If a man is in bed with a woman who is not his wife, and then the wife comes home and discovers
them, we say he was busted.
Busted can also be used for illegal activities.
For example, the pastor was busted stealing money from his church.
Or any activity that you're not supposed to be doing.
For example, my boss walked into my office while I was on Facebook.
I was busted.
Number nine, trashed, hammered, and wasted.
All mean drunk with alcohol.
There are a number of ways to say someone is drunk, but trashed, hammered, and wasted are
three of the most common.
The word wasted can also be used to describe someone under the influence of illegal drugs.
In the case of drugs, we also have two other words.
A person is high if they have taken a drug that makes them feel happy or excited, and
they are stoned if they have taken a drug that makes them feel relaxed.
Number ten, a hang up.
A hang up is an excessive preoccupation or obsession about some detail.
For example, if your roommate is obsessive about keeping all his DVDs in alphabetical order,
you could say he has a real hang up about it.
Another situation is if your boss insists that all attachments emailed to him be in PDF
format, not word format, then he definitely has a hang up about file formats.
Although a hang up can be a small and relatively unimportant detail, as in these examples, the
word can also refer to a genuine psychological obstacle that makes life difficult in some
way.
For example, people have a lot of hang ups about failure.
A lot of us are so afraid to fail that we won't even try.
Number eleven, mooch and freeload mean take advantage of the generosity of other people
to get something for free.
Imagine you have a friend who always eats some of your food in the restaurant, but never helps
pay the bill.
He always asks for rides because he doesn't have a car, and he lives with his parents but
doesn't contribute to the household expenses.
We call this person a mooch or a freeloader, or we say he's mooching off his parents and
friends.
It's not a compliment.
Number twelve, hassle means an annoying difficulty or to bother or annoy someone.
You can describe any complicated or bureaucratic procedure by saying it's such a hassle, because
not only is it difficult, but it's also annoying.
This word is also used as a verb.
For example, men sometimes hassle women on the street by making comments about their bodies.
Children often hassle their parents when the parents are trying to concentrate on something
else.
Number thirteen, yeah right, means I don't believe you.
This expression, like the second meaning of big deal, is a sarcastic one.
It's used to say you don't believe what the other person said.
You don't think it is true or probable.
For example, I'm in way better shape than you.
Yeah right, you can barely walk up the stairs without getting tired.
Maybe we'll get a raise this year.
Yeah right, the owners of the company want to keep all the profits for themselves.
Number fourteen, cool means great, popular or fashionable.
Cool is similar to awesome, although not quite as strong.
You can use it to describe objects, experiences and also people.
If you describe someone as cool, it generally means the person is relaxed and popular.
Number fifteen, cheesy or corny, mean something that is ridiculous, unpopular or stupid.
Cheesy and corny are the opposite of cool.
They describe something that is ridiculous and terribly unfashionable.
People would be embarrassed about it.
You can say a movie was cheesy if it had a typical and predictable story that didn't seem realistic,
interesting or imaginative.
There are hundreds of slang words in English and they're changing all the time.
Every year new slang words become popular and old expressions stop being used.
If you're watching a movie or TV show and you're having trouble with the slang, try
to understand the word or expression from its context.
For example, if a man is looking at a beautiful woman and says, she's so hot, then you can
guess that hot, in this case, is a slang word for beautiful or sexy.
You've finished lesson forty-four.
There's no quiz or speaking task for today, but here are some resources for further study
of slang.
Online slang dictionary dot com, urban dictionary dot com, and idiomquest dot com slash idioms.
You can find the links in the lesson text.
